claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Ta, Ti, V, and Zr solutes generate strong lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr.
The solute-induced lattice distortions lower the effective Peierls barrier.
A lower Peierls barrier facilitates dislocation nucleation and glide.
Easier dislocation nucleation and glide delay crack initiation and propagation relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed initial WTaTiVZr material has a homogeneous single-phase BCC matrix.
Lattice distortion gives WTaTiVZr elevated dislocation mobility at high temperature.
Finer grains or distributed short-range-order fluctuations may contribute to the alloy's high-temperature plastic response.
The proposed nanoscale microstructural enhancements are absent in pure tungsten.
Lowering the dislocation-motion barrier produces more uniform plastic flow.
Pure tungsten typically undergoes brittle crack initiation under the proposed service conditions.
More active dislocation mechanisms increase plastic-strain capacity and toughness.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a statistically significant increase in plastic strain under identical 1000–1200 °C testing relative to pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit statistically significantly higher fracture toughness under identical 1000–1200 °C testing relative to pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will have a higher dislocation density and more active dislocation motion than pure tungsten after high-temperature testing.
The proposed mechanism is primarily valid near or above 1000 °C because thermal activation assists dislocation motion.
Phase instability or oxidation can confound the proposed lattice-distortion mechanism.
Microstructural state, including matrix ordering and nanoscale secondary regions, can strongly affect ductility in refractory multicomponent alloys.
Higher dislocation density or enhanced mobility would indicate a reduced dislocation activation barrier.
